prompt: `CER1K` brings in 41.5% of the revenue and `SUL1K` 40.9%. Why does the lesson draw the six products as sorted bars rather than a pie?
hint: What does the eye compare in each?

choices.text: A pie draws at most four slices
choices.why: Excel draws a pie of six slices without complaint; the trouble is reading it.

choices.text: Lengths on one baseline read better than angles
choices.why: Right. In the pie the two big slices look equal; in the bars the R$ 274 lead shows.

choices.text: Bars are the only chart a PivotChart can draw
choices.why: A PivotChart can be a pie too; the choice is about the reader.

choices.text: Pies always round the percentages to whole numbers
choices.why: Nothing is rounded; the problem is that angles are hard to compare.

prompt: What does `=SUMIFS(Sales[Revenue], Sales[Product], "CER1K")-SUMIFS(Sales[Revenue], Sales[Product], "SUL1K")` return?
hint: The gap the pie hides.

prompt: Somebody draws revenue by product as a line chart, `CER1K` to `SUL250`. What is wrong with it?
hint: What does joining two points claim?

choices.text: Nothing, since a line and a column chart show the same values
choices.why: The values are the same; the line adds a claim the data does not make.

choices.text: Excel won't draw a line over text
choices.why: It can and will; that is how the mistake gets made.

choices.text: It draws a trend between products, which have no order
choices.why: Right. A line suits months, which follow one another; products come in no order.

choices.text: The line should have been drawn with markers on every point
choices.why: Markers do not remove the false trend the joining line draws.

prompt: Match each question to the form that answers it.
hint: One form answers none of them well.

pairs.left: How did revenue change month by month?
Do bags and price move together, sale by sale?

prompt: What does `=MINIFS(Sales[Bags], Sales[Channel], "Wholesale")` return, the smallest wholesale sale in bags?
hint: Run it on your table.

prompt: Why does the lesson chart a small summary rather than the table `Sales` itself?
hint: How many points would a chart of the table have?

choices.text: Excel refuses to chart a range longer than 100 rows
choices.why: It charts far longer ranges; it would draw every sale.

choices.text: It would draw all 108 sales; a chart needs totals
choices.why: Right. A summary of formulas or a pivot table adds them up first, and the chart draws the answer.

choices.text: A table cannot be the source of any chart
choices.why: A table can be a source, and grows the chart when rows are added. It just needs to be a summary.

choices.text: Charts read only values, never formulas
choices.why: Charts draw the values formulas return; the Monthly sheet is all formulas.

prompt: How many wholesale sales does the `COUNTIFS` of the section find from 1 April to 31 May 2026?
hint: It explains the fall in the line.

prompt: The pivot table is sorted largest first, yet the Clustered Bar PivotChart shows `CER1K`, the largest, at the bottom. What fixes it?
hint: A bar chart draws its first category next to the axis.

choices.text: Sort the pivot table smallest first and refresh
choices.why: That works by accident and leaves the pivot table itself upside down for anyone reading it.

choices.text: Delete the chart and insert a Clustered Column instead
choices.why: Columns would read left to right, but the long product names suit bars; there is a direct fix.

choices.text: Tick Categories in reverse order in Format Axis
choices.why: Right. The first category then sits at the top, where a reader starts.

choices.text: Refresh the PivotChart, which still holds the old order
choices.why: Nothing is stale; the bottom-up order is how a bar chart draws.

prompt: Why can a PivotChart never be a scatter of bags against price?
hint: What does a scatter need, and what does a pivot table give?

choices.text: The sales are already added up
choices.why: Right. For a scatter, chart a range of records, not a summary.

choices.text: Scatters need dates on the horizontal axis
choices.why: A scatter takes any numbers on both axes; bags and price are both numbers.

choices.text: PivotCharts can only use the Sum function
choices.why: A PivotChart draws whatever the pivot summarises, average or count included.

choices.text: Slicers cannot be connected to a scatter
choices.why: That is not the reason; the chart type is simply not offered for a PivotChart.

prompt: Put the building of the `Monthly` line chart in order.
hint: Dates first, then what is added up for each, then the check, then the chart.
items: Type the headers and 2025-01-01 in A2
Put =EDATE(A2,1) in A3 and fill it down to A19
Put the two SUMIFS in B2 and C2 and fill them down
Select A1:B19 and insert a Line chart
trap: Charting before checking draws a wrong number as confidently as a right one.

prompt: With the value axis starting at 10,000, how many times taller is the `Wholesale` bar drawn than the `Online` bar? One decimal.
hint: Subtract 10,000 from each, then divide.

prompt: Why must the value axis of a bar or column chart start at zero?
hint: What does the eye read off a bar?

choices.text: Because Excel cannot set any other minimum on a bar chart
choices.why: Format Axis lets you set any minimum, which is exactly how the mistake is made.

choices.text: The eye reads a bar's length as its value
choices.why: Right. From 10,000, a 3.48 times lead is drawn 25 times taller.

choices.text: Values below it would show as errors
choices.why: It does not error; the bar just disappears below the axis, as the shop's did.

choices.text: Because a line chart beside it must start at zero too
choices.why: A line may start above zero; its reader follows positions, not lengths.

prompt: The Mix chart is going into a monthly report. Which title serves its reader best?
hint: The reader should know what to look for before looking.

choices.text: Revenue
choices.why: That repeats the axis and tells the reader nothing to look for.

choices.text: Chart 1
choices.why: It names the chart and not what it shows.

choices.text: Revenue by channel, all data
choices.why: Better, but a report title should name the period, and this one can state the finding.

choices.text: Wholesale brings in three quarters of the revenue
choices.why: Right. It states the finding, and the bars let anybody check it.

prompt: Which of these improve the single-series Mix chart? Choose all that apply.
hint: Each element should help the reader see the answer.

choices.text: Data labels on the bars, with the gridlines then deleted
choices.why: Three written values say more than gridlines the eye has to follow.

choices.text: Deleting the legend
choices.why: One series needs no legend; the title says what is plotted.

choices.text: Setting the axis minimum to 10,000 to show the differences better
choices.why: It shows them falsely: lengths stop matching values and the shop vanishes.

choices.text: A different colour for every bar, with nothing saying why
choices.why: Colour with no meaning invites the reader to look for one. Use a second colour once, for a reason the title names.

prompt: The length of a bar is its value, so the value axis of a bar chart starts at ___.
hint: A number.

prompt: When is a combo chart honest, by the lesson's rule?
hint: Compare revenue with its average, and revenue with bags.

choices.text: When both are in one unit, on one axis
choices.why: Right. Revenue and its three-month average are both reais, so one axis serves both.

choices.text: Only when one of the series is a line
choices.why: Every combo chart has a line; that is not what makes it honest.

choices.text: When the second axis is set to start at zero
choices.why: Zero helps, but the second axis's top is still a free choice that moves the line.

choices.text: Whenever Excel picks the bounds of both axes itself
choices.why: Excel's own choice is still a choice nobody explains to the reader.

prompt: In the two charts of revenue and bags, the line follows the columns in one and lies flat in the other. What differs between them?
hint: The data is the same in both.

choices.text: The second chart leaves out the wholesale sales
choices.why: Both draw every sale; the columns are identical.

choices.text: Only the bounds of the right-hand axis: 0 to 60, then 0 to 200
choices.why: Right. Where the line sits is set by that choice, not by the data.

choices.text: The first uses bags and the second uses revenue per bag
choices.why: Both draw bags; nothing else changed.

choices.text: The second chart is a PivotChart and follows a slicer
choices.why: Neither is a PivotChart; both come from the Monthly sheet.

prompt: What is the three-month average in D19, for April to June 2026?
hint: AVERAGE of B17:B19.

prompt: A manager wants to see how revenue and bags relate month by month. What does the lesson suggest instead of a second axis?
hint: One of the two ways divides one series by the other.

choices.text: A pie for each month
choices.why: A pie shows parts of one whole; it relates neither measure to the other.

choices.text: Bags as columns and revenue as the line, swapped
choices.why: Swapping which series is on the second axis keeps the free choice of its bounds.

choices.text: Revenue per bag, or two stacked charts
choices.why: Right. A ratio has one unit, and stacked charts let nobody choose where one line sits against the other.

choices.text: A line for both on one axis, with no secondary axis at all
choices.why: On one axis the bags would lie flat at the bottom, from 14 to 51 against thousands of reais.

prompt: What is the highest monthly revenue per bag in E2:E19, in reais? Two decimals.
hint: `=MAX(E2:E19)`, or read March 2026.

prompt: Looking down column T with the default settings, `CER250` seems as busy as `CER1K`. Why?
hint: Its best month was 6 bags; CER1K's was 39.

choices.text: Every sparkline is scaled to its own highest and lowest values
choices.why: Right. Each line fills its cell whatever its size, so shape shows and size hides.

choices.text: CER250 really did sell as many bags as CER1K
choices.why: It sold 24 bags in all against 200; the drawing hides the difference.

choices.text: Sparklines round small numbers up to make them visible
choices.why: Nothing is rounded; it is the scale, set per line.

choices.text: The grid's mixed references copied CER1K's numbers into CER250's row
choices.why: The SUMIFS grid checks out at 591 bags; each row holds its own product.

prompt: A reader wants to compare the six products' months by size. Which axis setting should the sparklines use?
hint: Sparkline › Axis.

choices.text: Automatic for Each Sparkline, the default
choices.why: That fits a reader asking about each product's shape, not one comparing sizes.

choices.text: A Win/Loss type instead of a line
choices.why: Win/Loss shows only above or below zero, and every month here is zero or more.

choices.text: High Point switched on
choices.why: It marks each line's best month, on that line's own scale.

choices.text: Same for All Sparklines, for both the minimum and the maximum
choices.why: Right. Every line then runs from 0 to 39 bags and sizes can be compared.

prompt: In the grid formula, `$A2` keeps column A fixed while the formula is filled right, and `B$1` keeps the ___ of the dates fixed while it is filled down.
hint: Number 1, the one with the months.

prompt: Somebody selects T2:T7 and presses Delete, and the sparklines are still there. What removes them?
hint: A sparkline belongs to its cell, but it is not the cell's value.

choices.text: Deleting column T's values with Clear Contents
choices.why: That is what Delete already did; the sparklines are not contents.

choices.text: Sparkline › Clear
choices.why: Right. Sparklines are removed from the Sparkline tab, not with the Delete key.

choices.text: Undoing the SUMIFS grid in B2:S7
choices.why: The lines would then draw zeros; they would not go away.

choices.text: Selecting them as shapes and pressing Delete again
choices.why: They are not shapes floating over the sheet, so they cannot be selected as one.

prompt: A colleague charts monthly wholesale revenue as columns and monthly online revenue as a line on a secondary axis, and says online sales track wholesale closely. What do you tell them?
hint: Both series are in reais.

choices.text: The line's position comes from a second axis they set; put both on one axis or in two charts
choices.why: Right. Both are reais, so one axis is honest; on two, how closely they track is whatever the bounds make it.

choices.text: They are right, since the line follows the columns
choices.why: On a second axis it follows the columns because of where its bounds were put.

choices.text: They should switch the line to columns on the same secondary axis
choices.why: The second axis stays a free choice whatever form the series takes.

choices.text: They should add data labels to every point so the reader can check
choices.why: Labelling every point clutters the chart and leaves the misleading scale in place.

prompt: A report needs the revenue of the eleven customers, from largest to smallest. Which chart fits?
hint: Eleven amounts to compare, with names on them.

choices.text: A pie with eleven slices
choices.why: Eleven angles cannot be compared, and the small slices become slivers.

choices.text: A line through the eleven customers
choices.why: Customers have no order, so a line would draw a trend that does not exist.

choices.text: A combo chart with revenue on two axes
choices.why: One measure needs one axis; a second adds nothing but a free choice.

choices.text: Sorted bars
choices.why: Right. Many named categories to compare is the case bars are for.
